questions: What is an operating system and what are its main functions?
Why do we need an operating system at all? Couldn't programs talk to the hardware directly?
keyPoints: Acts as an intermediary between user programs and hardware
Resource manager: allocates CPU, memory, storage and I/O devices among programs
Provides abstractions such as processes, files and virtual memory so programs don't deal with raw hardware
Provides protection and isolation between programs and users
Core functions: process management, memory management, file system, device management, security
entries.referenceAnswer: An operating system is system software that sits between applications and hardware. It manages resources like CPU time, memory, disks and devices, and shares them safely among many programs. It also provides clean abstractions such as processes, files and virtual address spaces, so programs don't have to control hardware directly, and it enforces protection so one program can't corrupt another.
commonMistakes: Describing only the user interface (GUI/shell) as the OS
Leaving out protection and isolation

questions: What is the difference between a monolithic kernel and a microkernel?
Why don't all operating systems use a microkernel if it is more reliable?
keyPoints: Monolithic kernel: all OS services (file system, drivers, memory, scheduling) run in kernel space, e.g. Linux
Microkernel: only minimal services (IPC, basic scheduling, low-level memory) in kernel; others run as user-space servers, e.g. Minix, QNX
Monolithic is faster because services call each other directly
Microkernel is more reliable and modular: a crashing driver doesn't bring down the kernel
Microkernel pays a performance cost for message passing / IPC between services
Hybrid kernels (Windows NT, macOS XNU) mix both approaches
entries.referenceAnswer: In a monolithic kernel, like Linux, all core services run together in kernel space, so they can call each other directly and performance is high. A bug in any driver, though, can crash the whole system. A microkernel keeps only the bare minimum in the kernel, like IPC and basic scheduling, and runs file systems and drivers as user-space processes. That improves isolation and reliability, but every service interaction becomes an IPC message, which adds overhead. That overhead is why most mainstream systems are monolithic or hybrid.
commonMistakes: Saying microkernels are always faster
Not mentioning the IPC overhead trade-off

questions: What is the difference between user mode and kernel mode?
Why does the CPU need two modes of operation?
keyPoints: A mode bit in the CPU indicates the current mode
Kernel mode can execute privileged instructions and access all memory and hardware
User mode is restricted; privileged instructions cause a trap
User programs enter kernel mode only through system calls, interrupts or exceptions
Dual mode protects the OS and other programs from buggy or malicious user code
entries.referenceAnswer: The CPU has a mode bit that separates kernel mode from user mode. In kernel mode code can run privileged instructions, like I/O and changing page tables, and access any memory. In user mode those instructions are forbidden, and trying them traps to the OS. Applications run in user mode and switch to kernel mode only in a controlled way, through system calls, interrupts or exceptions. This is what stops a faulty program from taking over the machine.
commonMistakes: Thinking user programs can switch to kernel mode directly
Confusing kernel mode with running as the admin/root user

questions: What is a system call? Give some examples.
What happens step by step when a program makes a system call like read()?
keyPoints: A system call is the programmatic interface through which a user program requests a service from the kernel
Implemented via a trap/software interrupt that switches the CPU to kernel mode
The kernel looks up the handler using the system call number, executes it, then returns to user mode
Categories: process control (fork, exit), file management (open, read, write), device management, information, communication
Library functions like printf are wrappers that eventually invoke system calls like write
entries.referenceAnswer: A system call is how a user program asks the kernel to do something privileged, like reading a file or creating a process. The program puts the system call number and arguments in registers and executes a trap instruction. That switches the CPU to kernel mode and jumps to the kernel's handler. The kernel validates the arguments, does the work, puts the result in a register and returns to user mode. Examples are fork, exec, open, read, write and exit.
commonMistakes: Treating library functions like printf as system calls themselves
Forgetting the mode switch

questions: What is an interrupt, and how is it different from a trap?
Why is interrupt-driven I/O better than polling, and where does DMA come in?
keyPoints: Interrupt: asynchronous signal from hardware (e.g. disk done, keyboard press, timer)
Trap/exception: synchronous, caused by the running instruction (system call, divide by zero, page fault)
On an interrupt the CPU saves state and jumps to the handler via the interrupt vector table
Polling wastes CPU cycles repeatedly checking device status
DMA lets a device transfer a whole block directly to memory and interrupt the CPU only once at the end
The timer interrupt is what lets the OS preempt processes
entries.referenceAnswer: An interrupt is an asynchronous signal from hardware, like a disk finishing a read. A trap is synchronous: it's caused by the instruction currently executing, like a system call or a divide-by-zero. In both cases the CPU saves its state and jumps to a handler through the interrupt vector table. Interrupts beat polling because the CPU does useful work instead of repeatedly checking a device. For bulk transfers, DMA goes further: the controller copies data straight to memory and interrupts only once when the whole block is done, instead of once per byte.
commonMistakes: Calling a page fault an interrupt from a device
Not knowing the timer interrupt enables preemptive scheduling

questions: What is the difference between a program and a process?
What does a process look like in memory?
keyPoints: A program is a passive file on disk; a process is a program in execution
One program can have many processes running at once
Process memory layout: text (code), data (globals), heap (dynamic, grows up), stack (function calls, grows down)
A process also has execution state: program counter, registers, open files, and a PCB in the kernel
entries.referenceAnswer: A program is a passive set of instructions stored on disk. A process is an active instance of that program being executed, with its own state. The same program, say a browser, can run as several processes. In memory a process has a text section for code, a data section for global variables, a heap for dynamic allocation, and a stack for function calls and local variables. The kernel tracks it through a process control block that holds the program counter, registers and open files.
commonMistakes: Saying heap and stack are the same thing
Forgetting a program can map to multiple processes

questions: What are the different states of a process?
What causes a process to move from running back to ready, versus from running to waiting?
keyPoints: States: New, Ready, Running, Waiting (Blocked), Terminated
Ready to Running: the scheduler dispatches the process
Running to Ready: preempted, e.g. time slice expires or a higher-priority process arrives
Running to Waiting: the process requests I/O or waits for an event
Waiting to Ready: the I/O completes or the event occurs (never directly to Running)
Some systems add suspended states when processes are swapped out
entries.referenceAnswer: A process moves through New, Ready, Running, Waiting and Terminated. It becomes Ready once admitted, and the scheduler dispatches it to Running. From Running it goes back to Ready if it is preempted, for example when its time quantum expires. It goes to Waiting if it asks for I/O or waits on an event. When that event completes it returns to Ready, not straight to Running, because it has to be scheduled again. Finishing moves it to Terminated.
commonMistakes: Saying a process goes from Waiting directly to Running
Confusing preemption (to Ready) with blocking (to Waiting)

questions: What is a Process Control Block and what does it contain?
Why does the OS need a PCB for every process?
keyPoints: The PCB is the kernel data structure representing a process
Contains process ID and state
Contains program counter and saved CPU registers
Contains scheduling info (priority, queue pointers)
Contains memory management info (page table / base-limit registers)
Contains accounting info and I/O status (open files list)
entries.referenceAnswer: The PCB is the kernel's record of a process. It holds the process ID and state, the saved program counter and registers, scheduling information like priority, memory-management information like the page table pointer, accounting data, and the list of open files and I/O devices. It's needed because when a process isn't running, its CPU state has to be stored somewhere, so it can resume exactly where it left off after a context switch.
commonMistakes: Thinking the PCB stores the program's code or data
Leaving out saved registers and the program counter

questions: What is a context switch and what happens during it?
Why is a context switch between threads of the same process cheaper than between two processes?
keyPoints: Saving the state of the current process into its PCB and loading the next process's state
Triggered by interrupts (e.g. timer), system calls that block, or preemption
Context switch time is pure overhead: no useful work is done
A process switch also changes the address space: page table base register, and often a TLB flush and cold caches
A thread switch within the same process keeps the address space, so it avoids the TLB flush and most cache effects
entries.referenceAnswer: A context switch happens when the CPU moves from one process to another. The kernel saves the current process's registers and program counter into its PCB, picks the next process, and restores that process's saved state. It's pure overhead, since no user work gets done during it. Switching between processes also means switching address spaces: loading a new page table base, often flushing the TLB, and running with cold caches afterward. Threads of the same process share one address space, so switching between them only swaps registers and stack. That's much cheaper.
commonMistakes: Missing the TLB and cache cost of a process switch
Saying a context switch copies the process's memory

questions: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
What do threads of the same process share, and what does each thread have of its own?
keyPoints: A thread is the smallest unit of CPU execution inside a process
Threads share the code, data, heap and open files of their process
Each thread has its own stack, program counter and registers
Threads are cheaper to create and switch than processes
Processes are isolated; a crash or memory bug in one thread can affect the whole process
Shared memory makes thread communication easy but requires synchronization
entries.referenceAnswer: A process is an independent program in execution with its own address space. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process. Threads of the same process share its code, data, heap and open files, but each has its own stack, program counter and registers. So threads are lighter: cheaper to create and switch, and they can communicate through shared memory. The downside is weaker isolation. One thread's bug can corrupt memory for all of them, and shared data needs synchronization.
commonMistakes: Saying threads share the stack
Saying threads have separate address spaces

questions: What is the difference between user-level and kernel-level threads?
Explain the many-to-one, one-to-one and many-to-many threading models.
keyPoints: User-level threads are managed by a user-space library; the kernel sees only one process
User-level threads are fast to create and switch, but if one blocks on a system call the whole process blocks
Kernel-level threads are known and scheduled by the kernel and can run in parallel on multiple cores
Many-to-one: many user threads on one kernel thread; no parallelism
One-to-one: each user thread maps to a kernel thread (Linux, Windows); true parallelism, higher creation cost
Many-to-many: multiplexes many user threads over a smaller or equal number of kernel threads
entries.referenceAnswer: User-level threads are managed entirely by a library in user space, so the kernel isn't aware of them. Switching is very fast, but a blocking system call blocks the whole process, and they can't use multiple cores. Kernel threads are scheduled by the OS, so they can block independently and run in parallel, at a higher cost per operation. The mapping models are many-to-one (no parallelism), one-to-one (used by Linux and Windows), and many-to-many, which multiplexes user threads over a pool of kernel threads.
commonMistakes: Saying user-level threads can run on multiple cores in parallel under many-to-one
Not knowing which model Linux uses

questions: What does the fork() system call do, and what does it return?
What is the difference between fork() and exec()?
If a program calls fork() three times in a row, how many processes are there in total?
keyPoints: fork() creates a child process that is a copy of the parent
It returns 0 in the child, the child's PID in the parent, and -1 on failure
Parent and child continue executing from the instruction after fork()
exec() replaces the current process image with a new program; it does not create a new process
The shell runs commands with fork() followed by exec() in the child
n consecutive fork() calls produce 2^n processes in total
Modern systems use copy-on-write so fork() doesn't copy memory immediately
entries.referenceAnswer: fork() creates a new child process that is a near-identical copy of the parent. Both continue from the next instruction, and they tell themselves apart by the return value: 0 in the child, the child's PID in the parent, -1 on error. exec() doesn't create a process at all. It replaces the current process's memory image with a new program. The shell combines them: it forks, and the child calls exec to become the command. Because every existing process forks again, n fork calls in a row give 2^n processes. Copy-on-write keeps fork cheap by sharing pages until someone writes.
commonMistakes: Saying exec() creates a new process
Mixing up which process gets 0 as the return value
Counting n+1 processes for n forks

questions: What is a zombie process? How is it different from an orphan process?
Why can zombie processes be a problem, and how are they cleaned up?
keyPoints: A zombie has finished executing but still has an entry in the process table because its parent hasn't called wait()
The entry keeps the exit status for the parent to collect
An orphan is a process whose parent terminated while it was still running
Orphans are adopted by init/systemd (PID 1), which reaps them when they exit
Many zombies can exhaust PIDs / process table slots
Fix: the parent calls wait()/waitpid(), handles SIGCHLD, or the parent is killed so init reaps the zombies
entries.referenceAnswer: A zombie is a process that has exited, but its parent hasn't yet called wait() to read its exit status, so its process-table entry stays around. An orphan is the reverse: a still-running process whose parent has died. Orphans get adopted by init (PID 1), which reaps them when they finish. A few zombies are harmless, but a buggy parent that never waits can pile up zombies until the system runs out of PIDs. The fix is for the parent to call wait or handle SIGCHLD. Killing the parent also works, since init then adopts and reaps the zombies.
commonMistakes: Thinking you can kill a zombie with kill -9
Saying zombies consume CPU or memory

questions: What are the different ways processes can communicate with each other?
Compare shared memory and message passing.
keyPoints: Two basic models: shared memory and message passing
Shared memory: a region mapped into both processes; very fast after setup but needs explicit synchronization
Message passing: kernel-mediated send/receive; simpler and works across machines, but each message costs a system call and copying
Mechanisms: pipes (unidirectional, usually related processes), named pipes/FIFOs, message queues, sockets, signals, shared memory segments
Processes need IPC because each has an isolated address space
entries.referenceAnswer: Since processes have separate address spaces, they need OS-provided IPC to cooperate. There are two main models. Shared memory maps the same region into both processes. It's the fastest option, since there's no kernel involvement per access, but you have to synchronize access yourself. Message passing goes through the kernel with send and receive calls. That's easier to get right and works across machines, but each message costs a system call and a copy. Concrete mechanisms include pipes, named pipes, message queues, sockets, signals and shared memory segments.
commonMistakes: Saying shared memory needs no synchronization
Not explaining why IPC is needed (address space isolation)

questions: What criteria are used to evaluate a CPU scheduling algorithm?
What is the difference between turnaround time, waiting time and response time?
keyPoints: CPU utilization: keep the CPU busy (maximize)
Throughput: processes completed per unit time (maximize)
Turnaround time: completion time minus arrival time (minimize)
Waiting time: total time spent in the ready queue = turnaround minus burst time (minimize)
Response time: time from arrival until first getting the CPU (important for interactive systems)
Goals conflict, e.g. good response time vs high throughput
entries.referenceAnswer: Schedulers are judged on CPU utilization and throughput, which we want high, and on turnaround, waiting and response time, which we want low. Turnaround is the total time from arrival to completion. Waiting time is the part of that spent sitting in the ready queue, so turnaround minus burst time. Response time is how long until the process first gets the CPU, which matters most for interactive programs. These goals pull against each other. Round robin, for example, improves response time at the cost of more context-switch overhead.
commonMistakes: Confusing response time with turnaround time
Including I/O time in waiting time

questions: What is the difference between preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling?
Give an example of each.
keyPoints: Non-preemptive: once a process gets the CPU it keeps it until it blocks or terminates
Preemptive: the OS can take the CPU away, e.g. on a timer interrupt or when a higher-priority process arrives
Non-preemptive examples: FCFS, non-preemptive SJF
Preemptive examples: Round Robin, SRTF, preemptive priority
Preemption gives better responsiveness but adds context switches and raises race-condition concerns on shared data
entries.referenceAnswer: In non-preemptive scheduling a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks voluntarily, as in FCFS or plain SJF. In preemptive scheduling the OS can interrupt a running process, typically on a timer interrupt or when a higher-priority process becomes ready, as in Round Robin and SRTF. Preemption is what modern interactive systems use, because it stops one process hogging the CPU. It costs more context switches and means kernel data structures must be protected against concurrent access.
commonMistakes: Calling Round Robin non-preemptive
Thinking preemption means the process is terminated

questions: How does First-Come First-Served scheduling work, and what is its main drawback?
What is the convoy effect?
keyPoints: FCFS runs processes in order of arrival; non-preemptive; simple FIFO queue
Average waiting time can be very high and depends heavily on arrival order
Convoy effect: short processes wait behind one long CPU-bound process
Causes poor CPU and I/O device utilization
No starvation: every process eventually runs
entries.referenceAnswer: FCFS simply runs processes in the order they arrive, using a FIFO queue, and never preempts. It's easy to implement and never starves anyone. Its big problem is the convoy effect: if a long CPU-bound job arrives first, every short job queues behind it, and average waiting time shoots up. Meanwhile I/O devices sit idle because the I/O-bound processes can't get the CPU to issue their next request.
commonMistakes: Saying FCFS causes starvation
Not being able to explain the convoy effect with an example

questions: What is Shortest Job First scheduling, and why is it hard to implement in practice?
How does SRTF differ from SJF?
keyPoints: SJF picks the process with the smallest next CPU burst
SJF gives the minimum average waiting time for a given set of processes
SRTF is the preemptive version: a newly arrived job with a shorter remaining time preempts the running one
Problem: the length of the next CPU burst is not known in advance
Burst length is predicted, e.g. with exponential averaging of previous bursts
Long jobs can starve if short jobs keep arriving
entries.referenceAnswer: SJF always runs the process with the shortest next CPU burst. It's provably optimal for average waiting time, because running short jobs first lowers the wait for everyone behind them. SRTF is its preemptive form: if a new process arrives with less remaining time than the current one, it preempts it. The practical catch is that the OS can't know future burst lengths, so it has to estimate them, typically by exponential averaging of past bursts. SJF also risks starving long jobs if short ones keep arriving.
commonMistakes: Claiming SJF is optimal for turnaround of every individual process
Not mentioning starvation or burst prediction

questions: How does Round Robin scheduling work?
How does the choice of time quantum affect Round Robin's performance?
keyPoints: Each process runs for at most one time quantum, then is preempted and moved to the back of the ready queue
Preemptive, fair, and gives good response time; no starvation
If the quantum is very large, RR degenerates to FCFS
If the quantum is very small, context-switch overhead dominates
Rule of thumb: the quantum should be larger than most CPU bursts (e.g. about 80% of bursts finish within one quantum)
Average waiting time is often higher than SJF
entries.referenceAnswer: Round Robin gives each ready process the CPU for a fixed time quantum. If the process isn't done when its quantum expires, a timer interrupt preempts it and it goes to the back of the queue. That makes it fair, starvation-free and responsive, which is why it suits time-sharing systems. The quantum is the key tuning knob. Too large and RR behaves like FCFS. Too small and the CPU spends much of its time context switching. It's usually set so that most CPU bursts complete within one quantum.
commonMistakes: Saying a smaller quantum is always better
Forgetting that RR is preemptive

questions: What is priority scheduling and what problem can it cause?
What is aging and how does it solve starvation?
keyPoints: The CPU is given to the highest-priority ready process; can be preemptive or non-preemptive
SJF is a special case where priority is the predicted burst length
Starvation (indefinite blocking): low-priority processes may never run
Aging gradually increases the priority of processes that have waited a long time
Aging guarantees every process eventually runs
entries.referenceAnswer: Priority scheduling always runs the highest-priority ready process, either preemptively or not. SJF is actually a special case where priority is the predicted burst length. The risk is starvation: if high-priority work keeps arriving, low-priority processes may wait forever. Aging solves this by gradually raising the priority of processes the longer they wait, so every process eventually becomes important enough to run.
commonMistakes: Confusing starvation with deadlock
Proposing to fix starvation by lowering high priorities randomly

questions: How does a multilevel feedback queue scheduler work?
How does MLFQ favour interactive processes without knowing burst times in advance?
keyPoints: Several ready queues with different priorities, often with different time quanta
New processes start in the highest-priority queue
A process that uses its full quantum is demoted to a lower queue (CPU-bound behaviour)
A process that gives up the CPU early (I/O-bound, interactive) stays at high priority
Aging / periodic priority boost moves long-waiting processes up to prevent starvation
It learns process behaviour from history instead of needing burst times in advance
entries.referenceAnswer: MLFQ keeps several queues at different priority levels, with shorter quanta at higher levels. Every new process starts at the top. If a process burns through its whole quantum, it looks CPU-bound and is moved down a level. If it blocks for I/O before the quantum ends, it looks interactive and stays high. So the scheduler learns each process's behaviour from what it actually does, approximating SJF without knowing burst times ahead of time. To avoid starving CPU-bound jobs at the bottom, it periodically boosts or ages them back up.
commonMistakes: Describing plain multilevel queue (fixed queues) instead of feedback
Missing the starvation fix

questions: What is a race condition? Can you give an example?
Why can count++ on a shared variable produce a wrong result with two threads?
keyPoints: A race condition occurs when the result depends on the timing/interleaving of concurrent accesses to shared data
count++ is not atomic: it is load, increment, store
Two threads can both load the same old value and one update is lost
Prevented by making the critical section mutually exclusive (locks, semaphores, atomic operations)
entries.referenceAnswer: A race condition happens when several threads access shared data concurrently, at least one writes, and the outcome depends on exactly how their operations interleave. The classic example is count++. It's really three machine steps: load count into a register, add one, store it back. If two threads both load 5, both compute 6 and both store 6, one increment is lost. The fix is to make the update atomic, by protecting it with a lock or using an atomic instruction.
commonMistakes: Thinking count++ is a single atomic instruction
Saying race conditions only happen on multi-core machines

questions: What is the critical section problem?
What three requirements must a solution to the critical section problem satisfy?
keyPoints: The critical section is the part of code that accesses shared resources
Mutual exclusion: at most one process in the critical section at a time
Progress: if no one is in the critical section, the choice of who enters next can't be postponed indefinitely, and only processes wanting to enter take part in deciding
Bounded waiting: there is a limit on how many times others can enter before a waiting process gets its turn
Structure: entry section, critical section, exit section, remainder section
entries.referenceAnswer: A critical section is code that touches shared data, and the critical section problem is designing an entry and exit protocol so processes can use it safely. A correct solution needs three properties. Mutual exclusion: only one process inside at a time. Progress: if the section is free and someone wants in, the decision can't be delayed forever, and processes in their remainder section don't block it. Bounded waiting: a process waiting to enter can only be overtaken a limited number of times, so it can't starve.
commonMistakes: Listing only mutual exclusion
Confusing progress with bounded waiting

questions: Explain Peterson's solution to the critical section problem.
Why might Peterson's solution not work on modern processors?
keyPoints: Software solution for two processes using a flag[2] array and a turn variable
A process sets its own flag to true, gives the turn to the other, then waits while the other's flag is true and it is the other's turn
Satisfies mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting
Uses busy waiting
Can fail on modern CPUs/compilers that reorder memory operations unless memory barriers are used
entries.referenceAnswer: Peterson's solution works for two processes using two shared variables: a flag array, where each process announces it wants to enter, and a turn variable. To enter, process i sets flag[i] to true, then politely sets turn to the other process, and busy-waits while the other's flag is true and it's the other's turn. Whoever wrote turn last ends up waiting, so mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting all hold. On modern hardware, though, the CPU or compiler may reorder those reads and writes, which breaks the proof unless you add memory barriers. That's why real systems use hardware atomic instructions instead.
commonMistakes: Claiming it works for any number of processes as written
Not knowing about instruction reordering

questions: What is the difference between a mutex and a semaphore?
Is a binary semaphore the same as a mutex?
keyPoints: A mutex is a locking mechanism with ownership: only the thread that locked it may unlock it
A semaphore is an integer counter with wait (P) and signal (V) operations; it has no ownership
A counting semaphore allows up to N concurrent holders, e.g. a pool of N resources
A binary semaphore (0/1) is similar to a mutex but any thread can signal it, so it is also used for signalling between threads
A mutex is for mutual exclusion; a semaphore is for resource counting and synchronization/signalling
entries.referenceAnswer: A mutex is a lock with ownership: the thread that acquires it must be the one that releases it, and it guards a critical section. A semaphore is an integer with wait and signal operations and no ownership. Any thread can signal it. A counting semaphore lets up to N threads use a pool of N resources, and a binary semaphore holds only 0 or 1. A binary semaphore can be used like a mutex, but because it has no owner it's also used for signalling, like one thread telling another that data is ready, which a mutex shouldn't be used for.
commonMistakes: Saying a binary semaphore and a mutex are exactly identical
Not mentioning ownership

questions: How do the wait and signal operations of a semaphore work?
How can semaphores be implemented without busy waiting?
keyPoints: wait(S)/P: decrement S; if the result is negative, the process blocks
signal(S)/V: increment S; if processes are waiting, wake one of them
wait and signal must themselves be atomic
Busy-waiting semaphores (spinlocks) waste CPU
Blocking implementation: each semaphore has a queue of waiting processes; block() and wakeup() replace spinning
With a blocking implementation, a negative value's magnitude equals the number of waiting processes
entries.referenceAnswer: wait decrements the semaphore, and if the value would go below zero the caller has to wait. signal increments it and, if someone is waiting, wakes one of them. Both operations must be atomic. A naive implementation spins in a loop, wasting CPU. The blocking version attaches a queue to each semaphore: a process that can't proceed is put on the queue and sleeps, and signal takes one off the queue and makes it ready. In that version a negative value tells you how many processes are waiting.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that wait/signal must be atomic
Mixing up which operation blocks

questions: How would you solve the producer-consumer problem using semaphores?
Why do we need three semaphores in the bounded buffer solution?
keyPoints: Producers add to a fixed-size buffer; consumers remove from it
empty semaphore, initialized to N: counts free slots
full semaphore, initialized to 0: counts filled slots
mutex (binary semaphore, 1): protects the buffer itself
Producer: wait(empty), wait(mutex), add, signal(mutex), signal(full); the consumer mirrors this
Order matters: taking the mutex before waiting on empty/full can deadlock
entries.referenceAnswer: Producers put items into a buffer of size N and consumers take them out, so we need to stop producers when it's full, stop consumers when it's empty, and protect the buffer itself. That's three semaphores: empty starting at N, full starting at 0, and a mutex starting at 1. A producer does wait(empty), wait(mutex), inserts, then signal(mutex) and signal(full). A consumer does wait(full), wait(mutex), removes, then signal(mutex) and signal(empty). The order matters: if you grab the mutex first and then block on empty, you hold the lock while sleeping and the consumer can never get in, which is a deadlock.
commonMistakes: Swapping the order of wait(mutex) and wait(empty)
Using only one semaphore

questions: Explain the readers-writers problem.
In the first readers-writers solution, why can writers starve, and how can that be fixed?
keyPoints: Multiple readers may read shared data at the same time; a writer needs exclusive access
First (reader-preference) solution: a read_count protected by a mutex; the first reader locks out writers and the last reader lets them in
In the reader-preference version, a steady stream of readers can starve writers
The writer-preference version stops new readers once a writer is waiting, which can starve readers instead
Real systems provide reader-writer locks
entries.referenceAnswer: Readers can safely share data concurrently, but a writer needs it exclusively. The classic reader-preference solution keeps a read_count protected by a mutex, plus a write lock. The first reader to arrive takes the write lock, so writers are shut out, and the last reader to leave releases it. The catch is that if readers keep arriving, the count never drops to zero and writers starve. The writer-preference variant blocks new readers as soon as a writer is waiting, which moves the starvation risk to readers. Fair versions queue both in arrival order.
commonMistakes: Giving readers exclusive access too
Not identifying who starves in each variant

questions: What is the dining philosophers problem and why can the naive solution deadlock?
How can you prevent deadlock in the dining philosophers problem?
keyPoints: Five philosophers, five chopsticks; each needs both neighbouring chopsticks to eat
Naive solution: each picks up the left then the right chopstick
If all pick up their left chopstick at once, everyone waits forever: circular wait, deadlock
Fix: allow at most four philosophers at the table at a time
Fix: asymmetric order, e.g. odd philosophers pick left first and even ones pick right first (breaks the circular wait)
Fix: pick up both chopsticks only if both are available (atomically, e.g. with a monitor)
Deadlock-free solutions can still starve a philosopher unless designed for fairness
entries.referenceAnswer: Five philosophers sit around a table with one chopstick between each pair, and each needs both neighbours' chopsticks to eat. If every philosopher picks up the left chopstick at the same moment, each then waits for the right one forever. That's a circular wait, so a deadlock. You can prevent it by breaking one of the deadlock conditions: seat at most four at a time, make one philosopher pick up in the opposite order so the cycle can't form, or only pick up chopsticks when both are free, done atomically with a monitor. You still need to watch for starvation even once deadlock is gone.
commonMistakes: Not linking the deadlock to circular wait
Assuming deadlock-free implies starvation-free

questions: What is a monitor, and how is it better than using semaphores directly?
How do condition variables work inside a monitor?
keyPoints: A monitor is a high-level synchronization construct: shared data plus the procedures that operate on it
Only one process can be active inside the monitor at a time; mutual exclusion is automatic
Condition variables let a process wait inside the monitor for a condition
x.wait() suspends the caller and releases the monitor; x.signal() resumes one waiting process (no effect if none are waiting)
Less error-prone than raw semaphores, where a misplaced wait/signal causes deadlocks or races
Java synchronized methods with wait/notify are monitor-like
entries.referenceAnswer: A monitor bundles shared data with the procedures that access it and guarantees that only one process executes inside at a time, so you get mutual exclusion without writing lock calls yourself. For waiting on a condition, like buffer not empty, it provides condition variables. wait suspends the process and releases the monitor so others can enter, and signal wakes one waiting process. Unlike a semaphore signal, it does nothing if nobody is waiting. The main advantage over semaphores is safety: with raw semaphores a single misplaced wait or signal causes a deadlock or race, which is very hard to debug. Java's synchronized methods with wait and notify are a practical example.
commonMistakes: Saying condition variable signal behaves like semaphore signal (it isn't remembered)
Forgetting that wait releases the monitor lock

questions: What is a spinlock and when is it appropriate to use one?
How do hardware instructions like test-and-set help implement locks?
keyPoints: A spinlock makes a waiting thread loop (spin) until the lock is free: busy waiting
Wastes CPU cycles while spinning
Good on multiprocessors when critical sections are very short: avoids the cost of a context switch
Bad on a single processor: the lock holder can't run while the waiter spins
Implemented with atomic hardware instructions such as test-and-set or compare-and-swap
entries.referenceAnswer: A spinlock is a lock where a waiting thread just loops, repeatedly checking until the lock becomes free. That's busy waiting, and it wastes CPU. It's still the right choice on a multi-core machine when critical sections are tiny, because spinning briefly costs less than two context switches to block and wake up. On a single CPU it's pointless, since the holder can't make progress while you spin. Spinlocks are built on atomic instructions like test-and-set or compare-and-swap, which read and modify a memory word in one uninterruptible step.
commonMistakes: Saying spinlocks are always bad
Not knowing the atomic instructions they rely on

questions: What is priority inversion?
How does priority inheritance solve priority inversion?
keyPoints: A high-priority task waits for a lock held by a low-priority task
A medium-priority task preempts the low-priority task, so the high-priority task effectively waits on the medium one
Can cause missed deadlines in real-time systems (e.g. the Mars Pathfinder resets)
Priority inheritance: the lock holder temporarily inherits the priority of the highest-priority waiter
Priority ceiling protocol is another solution
entries.referenceAnswer: Priority inversion happens when a high-priority task needs a lock held by a low-priority task, and then a medium-priority task preempts the low one. Now the high-priority task is stuck behind the medium one, even though it outranks it. The Mars Pathfinder rover kept resetting because of exactly this. The standard fix is priority inheritance: while the low-priority task holds a lock that a high-priority task wants, it temporarily runs at the high priority. That lets it finish, release the lock and drop back down. The priority ceiling protocol is an alternative.
commonMistakes: Leaving out the medium-priority task (that's what makes it an inversion)
Confusing it with starvation

questions: What is a deadlock? What conditions must hold for it to occur?
Why is mutual exclusion one of the necessary conditions for deadlock?
keyPoints: Deadlock: a set of processes each waiting for a resource held by another in the set, so none can proceed
Mutual exclusion: at least one resource is non-shareable
Hold and wait: a process holds some resources while waiting for others
No preemption: resources can't be forcibly taken away
Circular wait: a cycle of processes, each waiting for the next
All four must hold at the same time; breaking any one prevents deadlock
entries.referenceAnswer: A deadlock is when a set of processes are all blocked, each waiting for a resource that another one in the set holds, so none of them can ever continue. Four conditions must hold together. Mutual exclusion: resources can't be shared. Hold and wait: processes hold resources while requesting more. No preemption: nothing can be forcibly taken away. Circular wait: there's a cycle of processes, each waiting on the next. Mutual exclusion is necessary because if every resource could be shared, nobody would ever have to wait for anyone. Remove any one condition and deadlock becomes impossible.
commonMistakes: Listing Banker's algorithm or starvation as a condition
Saying any single condition is enough to cause deadlock

questions: What is the difference between deadlock and starvation?
What is a livelock?
keyPoints: Deadlock: processes wait for each other in a cycle; none can ever proceed without intervention
Starvation: a process waits indefinitely because others keep getting preference, while the system as a whole keeps making progress
Starvation can end if conditions change; deadlock never resolves by itself
Starvation is fixed by aging/fairness; deadlock by prevention, avoidance, or detection and recovery
Livelock: processes keep changing state in response to each other but make no progress (not blocked, but stuck)
entries.referenceAnswer: In a deadlock a group of processes are all blocked waiting on each other in a cycle, and nothing moves without outside intervention. Starvation is when one process keeps getting passed over. The system is still making progress, just never for that process, as with a low-priority job under priority scheduling. Starvation can end if the load changes and is fixed with aging or fair scheduling. Deadlock never resolves by itself. A livelock is a third case: processes aren't blocked and keep actively changing state, like two people stepping aside for each other in a corridor, but none of them ever makes real progress.
commonMistakes: Using deadlock and starvation interchangeably
Saying deadlock implies starvation of the whole system in the same sense

questions: How can deadlocks be prevented?
Which deadlock condition is the most practical to break, and how?
keyPoints: Prevention: design the system so at least one of the four conditions can never hold
Mutual exclusion: often impossible to remove (e.g. printers, mutex locks); spooling helps for some devices
Hold and wait: request all resources at once, or release everything before requesting more; causes low utilization and starvation
No preemption: take resources from a waiting process; only works for resources whose state can be saved (CPU, memory)
Circular wait: impose a global ordering on resources and request only in increasing order; the most practical
Different from avoidance (Banker's) and detection/recovery
entries.referenceAnswer: Prevention means making sure one of the four deadlock conditions can never hold. Mutual exclusion usually can't be removed, because things like locks and printers are inherently exclusive. Hold and wait can be broken by requesting all resources up front, but that wastes resources and can starve processes. No preemption can be broken by taking resources away, which only works for things whose state can be saved, like CPU or memory. The most practical option is breaking circular wait: number all resources and require every process to acquire them in increasing order, so a cycle can't form. Many real systems enforce lock ordering this way.
commonMistakes: Confusing prevention with avoidance (Banker's algorithm)
Suggesting removing mutual exclusion as a general fix

questions: What is a safe state, and how does the Banker's algorithm use it?
What are the limitations of the Banker's algorithm?
keyPoints: Deadlock avoidance: grant a request only if the system stays in a safe state
Safe state: there exists an order (safe sequence) in which every process can get its maximum need and finish
Unsafe does not mean deadlocked, but it could lead to deadlock
Data structures: Available, Max, Allocation, Need = Max - Allocation
Safety algorithm: repeatedly find a process whose Need <= Work, pretend it finishes and releases its allocation
Limitations: each process must declare its maximum needs in advance; fixed number of processes and resources; O(m x n^2) cost; rarely used in general-purpose OSes
entries.referenceAnswer: The Banker's algorithm avoids deadlock by granting a request only if the system will still be in a safe state afterward. A state is safe if there's some order in which every process can obtain its maximum remaining need and finish. It tracks Available, Max and Allocation, and computes Need as Max minus Allocation. To check safety, it repeatedly finds a process whose Need fits in the currently available resources, assumes it finishes and returns its allocation, and repeats. If all processes can finish this way, the state is safe. It's rarely used in real OSes because processes must declare their maximum needs in advance, the set of processes and resources is assumed fixed, and it's expensive to run on every request.
commonMistakes: Saying an unsafe state is a deadlock
Calling Banker's a prevention technique

questions: How can an OS detect a deadlock, and how can it recover?
Why do most operating systems simply ignore deadlocks?
keyPoints: Single instance per resource type: build a wait-for graph and look for a cycle
Multiple instances: use a detection algorithm similar to Banker's safety check on the current requests
Recovery: terminate all deadlocked processes, or terminate them one at a time until the cycle breaks
Recovery: preempt resources from a victim and roll it back; choose victims to minimize cost and avoid starvation
Ostrich approach: most OSes (Linux, Windows) ignore deadlocks because they are rare and prevention/avoidance is expensive; applications must handle it
entries.referenceAnswer: For resources with a single instance, the OS can maintain a wait-for graph and check for cycles. A cycle means deadlock. With multiple instances it runs a detection algorithm that resembles the Banker's safety check, but uses the current requests. To recover, it can kill all the deadlocked processes, kill them one by one until the cycle breaks, or preempt resources from a victim and roll it back, choosing victims carefully so the same process isn't always picked. In practice general-purpose OSes mostly ignore deadlocks, the so-called ostrich algorithm, because they're rare and constant prevention is costly. Databases do run detection, since lock deadlocks there are common.
commonMistakes: Saying a cycle always means deadlock even with multiple resource instances
Not knowing real OSes largely ignore deadlocks

questions: What is a resource allocation graph?
If a resource allocation graph has a cycle, is there definitely a deadlock?
keyPoints: Nodes are processes (circles) and resources (rectangles, with dots for instances)
Request edge: process to resource; assignment edge: resource to process
No cycle means no deadlock
If every resource has a single instance, a cycle means deadlock
With multiple instances, a cycle is necessary but not sufficient for deadlock
entries.referenceAnswer: A resource allocation graph has process nodes and resource nodes, where each resource can have several instances. An edge from a process to a resource is a request, and an edge from a resource to a process is an assignment. If the graph has no cycle, there's definitely no deadlock. If there is a cycle and every resource has only one instance, there's definitely a deadlock. But with multiple instances, a cycle only means deadlock is possible: another process outside the cycle might release an instance and break it.
commonMistakes: Saying any cycle always means deadlock
Mixing up the direction of request and assignment edges

questions: What is the difference between a logical address and a physical address?
What does the MMU do?
keyPoints: Logical (virtual) address: generated by the CPU / seen by the program
Physical address: the actual location in RAM
The Memory Management Unit (MMU) translates logical to physical addresses at run time
Simplest scheme: physical = logical + relocation (base) register, checked against a limit register
Lets each program believe it starts at address 0 and protects processes from each other
entries.referenceAnswer: A logical address is what the program and CPU work with. A physical address is the real location in RAM. The MMU, a hardware unit, translates between them on every memory access. In the simplest scheme it adds a relocation register to the logical address and checks it against a limit register. With paging it uses page tables. This lets each process see its own address space starting at zero, lets the OS place it anywhere in memory, and stops processes from reaching each other's memory.
commonMistakes: Saying the OS translates every address in software
Confusing virtual memory size with physical memory size

entries.concept: Contiguous allocation: first, best and worst fit
questions: Explain first fit, best fit and worst fit memory allocation.
Which of these strategies generally performs best?
keyPoints: Contiguous allocation gives each process one continuous block of memory
First fit: the first hole big enough; fastest
Best fit: the smallest hole big enough; leaves tiny unusable holes and needs a full search (unless sorted)
Worst fit: the largest hole; leaves big leftover holes but generally performs worst
First and best fit generally beat worst fit on speed and utilization; first fit is usually fastest
All suffer from external fragmentation
entries.referenceAnswer: With contiguous allocation each process needs one continuous block. First fit takes the first free hole that's large enough, so it's fast. Best fit takes the smallest hole that fits, which sounds efficient but leaves lots of tiny, useless fragments and needs a full search. Worst fit takes the largest hole, hoping the leftover stays usable, but in practice it does worst. Simulations generally show first fit and best fit beating worst fit, with first fit being faster. All three suffer from external fragmentation.
commonMistakes: Assuming best fit is always best
Forgetting that all of them cause external fragmentation

questions: What is the difference between internal and external fragmentation?
How can external fragmentation be reduced?
keyPoints: Internal fragmentation: wasted space inside an allocated block because the block is larger than requested (e.g. the last page in paging)
External fragmentation: enough total free memory exists but it is not contiguous
Contiguous allocation and segmentation cause external fragmentation
Paging eliminates external fragmentation but causes internal fragmentation (on average half a page per process)
Compaction shuffles memory to merge holes; needs dynamic relocation and is expensive
Non-contiguous allocation (paging) is the main fix
entries.referenceAnswer: Internal fragmentation is waste inside an allocated block: you asked for less than you were given, as with the unused tail of a process's last page. External fragmentation is when free memory adds up to enough, but it's scattered in small holes, so no single contiguous request fits. Variable-size schemes like contiguous allocation and segmentation suffer from external fragmentation. Paging eliminates external fragmentation, because any free frame will do, but it introduces internal fragmentation of about half a page per process on average. Compaction can also merge holes, but it's expensive and needs run-time relocation.
commonMistakes: Saying paging eliminates all fragmentation
Swapping the two definitions

questions: What is paging and how does address translation work in paging?
What problem does paging solve?
keyPoints: Logical memory is divided into fixed-size pages and physical memory into frames of the same size
A per-process page table maps page numbers to frame numbers
A logical address is split into page number (p) and offset (d); physical address = frame(p) * page size + d
Allows non-contiguous allocation, so there is no external fragmentation
Cost: a page table per process and an extra memory access per reference, reduced with a TLB
Also enables sharing and protection bits per page
entries.referenceAnswer: Paging splits a process's logical memory into fixed-size pages and physical memory into frames of the same size, and a page can go in any free frame. Each process has a page table mapping page numbers to frame numbers. The CPU splits every logical address into a page number and an offset, looks up the frame in the page table, and combines frame and offset into the physical address. Because pages don't need to be contiguous, paging removes external fragmentation. The costs are page table memory and an extra memory access for the lookup, which the TLB mostly hides.
commonMistakes: Saying pages and frames are different sizes
Claiming paging has no fragmentation at all

entries.concept: Multilevel, hashed and inverted page tables
questions: Why do we need multilevel page tables?
What is an inverted page table and what are its trade-offs?
keyPoints: A flat page table for a large address space is huge, e.g. 32-bit with 4 KB pages means 2^20 entries (~4 MB) per process
Multilevel (hierarchical) paging pages the page table itself; only the parts actually used need to exist
Multilevel tables cost extra memory accesses per translation (mitigated by the TLB)
Hashed page tables are common for address spaces larger than 32 bits
Inverted page table: one entry per physical frame (not per virtual page), storing <pid, page>; one table for the whole system
An inverted table saves memory but lookup requires searching (use hashing) and shared memory is harder
entries.referenceAnswer: A single flat page table is too big for large address spaces. With 32-bit addresses and 4 KB pages you need a million entries, about 4 MB, for every process, even if it only uses a little memory. Multilevel paging solves this by paging the page table itself: an outer table points to inner tables, and inner tables are only created for regions actually in use. The cost is extra memory lookups per translation, which the TLB mostly absorbs. An inverted page table flips it around: one entry per physical frame, recording which process and page occupy it, so there's a single system-wide table sized to physical RAM. It saves memory, but a lookup means searching for the process-and-page pair, usually through a hash table, and sharing pages between processes gets awkward.
commonMistakes: Saying multilevel tables make translation faster
Thinking an inverted page table has one entry per virtual page

questions: What is a TLB and why is it needed?
What happens to the TLB on a context switch?
keyPoints: Without a TLB, every memory access needs an extra access to the page table in memory
The TLB is a small, fast, associative hardware cache of recent page-to-frame translations
TLB hit: translation without accessing the page table; miss: walk the page table and insert the entry
Works well because of locality of reference; hit ratios are typically very high
Effective access time depends on the hit ratio
On a context switch the TLB must be flushed, unless entries are tagged with address-space identifiers (ASIDs)
entries.referenceAnswer: With paging, every memory access would need a second access to read the page table, which would double memory latency. The TLB is a small, very fast associative cache inside the MMU that stores recent page-to-frame translations. On a hit the translation is almost free. On a miss the hardware or OS walks the page table and caches the result. Thanks to locality of reference, hit rates are very high, so effective access time stays close to a single memory access. When the OS switches to another process, the old translations are wrong, so the TLB either gets flushed or its entries are tagged with address-space IDs, so entries from different processes can coexist.
commonMistakes: Confusing the TLB with the CPU data cache
Not knowing about flushes or ASIDs on context switch

questions: What is segmentation and how is it different from paging?
Why do many systems combine segmentation and paging?
keyPoints: Segmentation divides memory into variable-size logical units that match the programmer's view (code, stack, heap, functions)
A logical address is <segment number, offset>; the segment table stores a base and limit for each segment
Paging uses fixed-size units that are invisible to the programmer
Segmentation suffers from external fragmentation; paging from internal fragmentation
Segmentation makes protection and sharing per logical unit natural
Segmented paging combines them: segments for the logical view, paging each segment to avoid external fragmentation
entries.referenceAnswer: Segmentation splits a process into variable-size segments that match how programmers think about it: code, data, stack, and so on. An address is a segment number plus an offset, and the segment table holds each segment's base and limit, with the offset checked against the limit. Paging instead uses fixed-size pages that don't match any logical structure. Segmentation makes protection and sharing natural, for example a read-only code segment, but its variable sizes cause external fragmentation. Paging avoids that but causes internal fragmentation. Combining them, by paging each segment, gets the logical view of segmentation without its fragmentation problem.
commonMistakes: Saying segments are fixed-size
Mixing up which scheme causes which fragmentation

questions: What is virtual memory and what are its benefits?
How can a program larger than physical RAM still run?
keyPoints: Separates logical memory from physical memory; only the parts of a process currently needed must be in RAM
The rest stays on disk (swap/backing store) and is loaded on demand
Programs can be larger than physical memory
More processes can be in memory at once, so better CPU utilization
Isolation between processes, and easy sharing (shared libraries, copy-on-write)
Usually implemented with demand paging
entries.referenceAnswer: Virtual memory gives each process a large logical address space that doesn't have to be fully backed by RAM. Only the pages a process is actually using need to be in memory, and the rest sit on disk and are brought in when touched. That's how a program bigger than RAM can run: at any moment it only needs its working set loaded. The benefits are programs larger than physical memory, more processes in memory at once for better CPU utilization, isolation between processes, and easy sharing of things like libraries. It's normally implemented with demand paging.
commonMistakes: Saying virtual memory simply means using the disk as RAM
Forgetting that isolation is a key benefit

questions: What is demand paging?
Walk me through what happens when a page fault occurs.
keyPoints: Demand paging loads a page only when it is first accessed (lazy loading)
Each page table entry has a valid-invalid bit
Accessing an invalid page traps to the OS: a page fault
The OS checks whether the reference is legal; if not, it terminates the process (segmentation fault)
Otherwise: find a free frame (run page replacement if none), read the page from disk, update the page table, and restart the faulting instruction
Page faults are very expensive (disk access), so the fault rate must be very low
entries.referenceAnswer: Demand paging loads pages only when they're first touched, instead of loading the whole program. Each page table entry has a valid bit. If a process touches a page that's not in memory, the MMU traps to the OS with a page fault. The OS first checks whether the address is legal at all, and if it isn't, the process gets a segmentation fault. If it's legal, the OS finds a free frame, evicting a page with a replacement algorithm if none is free. It schedules a disk read to bring the page in, the process blocks meanwhile, and then it updates the page table and restarts the instruction that faulted. Because a disk access costs so much more than a memory access, even a tiny fault rate dominates effective access time.
commonMistakes: Thinking every page fault is an error that kills the process
Forgetting that the faulting instruction is restarted

entries.concept: Page replacement: FIFO, Optimal and LRU
questions: Explain FIFO, Optimal and LRU page replacement.
Why can't the Optimal algorithm be implemented, and why study it then?
How is LRU approximated in real systems?
keyPoints: FIFO: evict the oldest loaded page; simple, but can evict heavily used pages and suffers from Belady's anomaly
Optimal (OPT/MIN): evict the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future; lowest possible fault rate
OPT needs future knowledge, so it can't be implemented; it is a benchmark for comparing algorithms
LRU: evict the page not used for the longest time in the past; approximates OPT using locality
Exact LRU needs a timestamp or stack update on every memory access, which is too costly without hardware support
Approximations: reference bit, second-chance (clock) algorithm
LRU and OPT are stack algorithms and don't suffer from Belady's anomaly
entries.referenceAnswer: When memory is full, a page fault needs a victim. FIFO evicts the page that's been in memory longest. It's simple but ignores usage, so it can throw out a hot page, and it suffers from Belady's anomaly. Optimal evicts the page that won't be needed for the longest time in the future. That gives the fewest possible faults, but it needs to know the future, so it's only used as a yardstick to measure other algorithms against. LRU uses the past as a predictor instead: it evicts the page unused for the longest time, which works well thanks to locality. Exact LRU would need a timestamp or list update on every memory access, which is too expensive, so real systems approximate it with a reference bit and the clock (second-chance) algorithm.
commonMistakes: Saying LRU is optimal
Saying Optimal can be implemented with enough bookkeeping

questions: What is Belady's anomaly?
Which page replacement algorithms suffer from Belady's anomaly and which don't? Why?
keyPoints: Increasing the number of frames can increase the number of page faults
Occurs with FIFO (classic example: reference string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 gives 9 faults with 3 frames and 10 with 4)
LRU and Optimal do not suffer from it: they are stack algorithms
Stack property: the set of pages in memory with n frames is always a subset of the set with n+1 frames
entries.referenceAnswer: Belady's anomaly is the counter-intuitive case where giving a process more frames produces more page faults. It happens with FIFO. The classic reference string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 causes 9 faults with 3 frames but 10 with 4. LRU and Optimal are immune because they're stack algorithms: the pages held with n frames are always a subset of the pages held with n+1 frames, so adding a frame can never cause an extra fault. FIFO lacks that property, because what's in memory depends on arrival order rather than usage.
commonMistakes: Saying LRU suffers from Belady's anomaly
Not being able to explain the stack property

questions: What is thrashing, and why does it happen?
How can an operating system detect and prevent thrashing?
keyPoints: Thrashing: the system spends more time paging than executing
Happens when processes don't have enough frames for their working sets (the pages they are actively using)
Vicious cycle: CPU utilization drops, so the OS adds more processes to raise it, which causes even more faults
Working set model: give each process enough frames for its working set; if the total demand exceeds available frames, suspend a process
Page-fault-frequency control: give more frames to processes with a high fault rate, take frames from ones with a low rate
Fix: reduce the degree of multiprogramming, or add RAM
entries.referenceAnswer: Thrashing is when a system is so busy swapping pages in and out that it barely does any real work. It happens when processes don't have enough frames to hold their working sets, the pages they're actively using, so they fault constantly and evict each other's pages. It spirals: CPU utilization drops, a naive scheduler sees an idle CPU and admits more processes, and that makes the shortage worse. The fix is to control the degree of multiprogramming. The working-set model gives each process enough frames for its working set and suspends processes if total demand exceeds memory. Page-fault-frequency control gives frames to processes with a high fault rate and takes them from those with a low one.
commonMistakes: Suggesting adding more processes to fix low CPU utilization
Describing thrashing as simply having many page faults, without the cause

questions: What is copy-on-write and why is it useful?
How does copy-on-write make fork() efficient?
keyPoints: Parent and child initially share the same physical pages, marked read-only
When either writes to a shared page, a page fault occurs and the OS makes a private copy of just that page
Pages that are never written are never copied
Makes fork() fast, especially when it's followed immediately by exec()
Saves memory and time
entries.referenceAnswer: Copy-on-write delays copying memory until it's actually needed. After fork, instead of duplicating the parent's whole address space, parent and child share the same physical pages, all marked read-only. The moment either one writes to a page, the write triggers a fault, and the OS copies just that one page and gives the writer its own copy. Pages that are only read are never copied. This makes fork very cheap, which matters because a fork is usually followed immediately by exec, which would have thrown the copied memory away anyway.
commonMistakes: Saying fork always copies the entire address space
Not linking copy-on-write to page faults

questions: What are the different file allocation methods? Compare them.
Which allocation method supports fast random access, and why?
keyPoints: Contiguous: each file occupies consecutive blocks; fast sequential and random access; suffers external fragmentation and makes growing files hard
Linked: each block points to the next; no external fragmentation; random access is slow (must traverse); a lost pointer loses the rest
FAT is a linked variant that keeps all the links in a table, allowing faster lookups
Indexed: an index block holds pointers to all the file's blocks; supports random access and no external fragmentation; overhead of the index block
Unix inodes use indexed allocation with direct and indirect pointers
entries.referenceAnswer: There are three classic methods. Contiguous allocation stores a file in consecutive blocks. Sequential and random access are fast, but it causes external fragmentation, and files can't easily grow. Linked allocation chains blocks with pointers, so there's no external fragmentation, but reaching block n means walking n pointers, so random access is slow, and one corrupted pointer loses the rest of the file. FAT keeps those links in a separate table to speed that up. Indexed allocation gives each file an index block listing all its block addresses, so you get random access without fragmentation, at the cost of the index block. Unix inodes are indexed allocation with multiple levels.
commonMistakes: Saying linked allocation supports efficient random access
Not knowing that inodes use indexed allocation

questions: What is an inode and what information does it store?
What is the difference between a hard link and a soft link?
keyPoints: An inode stores a file's metadata: size, owner, permissions, timestamps, link count, and pointers to data blocks
The filename is NOT stored in the inode; directories map names to inode numbers
Block pointers: direct pointers plus single, double and triple indirect pointers, so small files are fast and large files are still supported
Hard link: another directory entry pointing to the same inode; the data remains until the link count reaches 0
Soft (symbolic) link: a separate file containing a path; it breaks if the target is deleted and can cross file systems
entries.referenceAnswer: An inode is the Unix data structure that describes a file: its size, owner, permissions, timestamps, link count and pointers to its data blocks. It deliberately does not contain the filename. Directories are just tables mapping names to inode numbers. The block pointers are a mix of direct pointers, for fast access to small files, and single, double and triple indirect pointers to support very large files. A hard link is just another name pointing to the same inode, so the file survives until every name is removed. A symbolic link is its own small file containing a path to the target, so it breaks if the target is deleted, but it can point across file systems and to directories.
commonMistakes: Saying the inode stores the filename
Mixing up hard and soft links

questions: Explain the common disk scheduling algorithms.
Why is SSTF not always a good choice, and how does SCAN fix that?
keyPoints: Goal: minimize seek time (head movement) on hard disks
FCFS: fair but lots of head movement
SSTF: serve the closest request next; reduces seek time but can starve far-away requests
SCAN (elevator): the head moves to one end serving requests, then reverses
C-SCAN: serves in one direction only, then jumps back to the start; gives more uniform waiting times
LOOK / C-LOOK: like SCAN / C-SCAN but only go as far as the last request, not the disk edge
Largely irrelevant for SSDs, which have no seek time
entries.referenceAnswer: Disk scheduling orders I/O requests to reduce head movement on spinning disks. FCFS is fair but zig-zags a lot. SSTF always serves the nearest request, which cuts seek time but can starve requests at the far edges if new ones keep arriving near the head. SCAN, the elevator algorithm, sweeps the head to one end and back, serving requests along the way, which bounds how long anyone waits. C-SCAN only serves in one direction and then jumps back, giving more uniform wait times. LOOK and C-LOOK are the same but turn around at the last pending request instead of the physical edge. On SSDs seek time doesn't exist, so these matter much less.
commonMistakes: Saying SSTF is optimal and starvation-free
Confusing SCAN with C-SCAN

questions: What is RAID? Explain RAID 0, 1 and 5.
Which RAID level would you choose for a database server, and why?
keyPoints: RAID combines multiple disks for performance and/or reliability
RAID 0: striping; best performance and full capacity, but no redundancy: any disk failure loses all data
RAID 1: mirroring; survives a disk failure, good reads, 50% capacity
RAID 5: striping with distributed parity; survives one disk failure; good capacity; slower writes (parity updates)
RAID 6: double parity, survives two disk failures
RAID 10: mirrored stripes; fast and redundant; common for databases
RAID is not a backup: it doesn't protect against deletion or corruption
entries.referenceAnswer: RAID combines several disks into one logical unit for speed, reliability or both. RAID 0 stripes data across disks: fastest and uses all capacity, but one failed disk loses everything. RAID 1 mirrors data, so it survives a failure and reads well, at the cost of half the capacity. RAID 5 stripes data with distributed parity: it survives one disk failure with little capacity lost, but every write also has to update parity, so writes are slower. RAID 6 adds a second parity block to survive two failures. For a write-heavy database, RAID 10 is a common choice because it's fast and redundant without the parity-write penalty. And RAID isn't a backup: deleting a file deletes it on every disk.
commonMistakes: Saying RAID 0 provides redundancy
Treating RAID as a backup

questions: What happens when you switch on a computer, up to the point the OS is running?
What is a bootloader?
keyPoints: Firmware (BIOS or UEFI) runs first from non-volatile memory and performs POST (power-on self-test)
Firmware finds a bootable device using the configured boot order
It loads the bootloader (e.g. GRUB, Windows Boot Manager) from the MBR or the EFI system partition
The bootloader loads the kernel (and an initial RAM disk) into memory and transfers control to it
The kernel initializes memory management, drivers and the scheduler, and mounts the root file system
The kernel starts the first user process, init/systemd (PID 1), which starts services and the login screen
entries.referenceAnswer: When power comes on, the CPU starts executing firmware, BIOS or UEFI, stored on the motherboard. It runs a power-on self-test, then looks through the boot order for a bootable device. From there it loads a small program called the bootloader, like GRUB, whose job is to load the OS kernel into memory, often with an initial RAM disk containing the drivers needed to reach the real disk. The kernel then takes over: it sets up memory management, initializes devices and the scheduler, and mounts the root file system. Finally it starts the first user-space process, init or systemd with PID 1, which launches all the other services and eventually the login screen.
commonMistakes: Saying the kernel is loaded directly by the BIOS with no bootloader
Forgetting the init/systemd step

entries.concept: Memory hierarchy and locality of reference
questions: What is the memory hierarchy, and why do caches work?
What is locality of reference? Explain temporal and spatial locality.
keyPoints: Hierarchy from fastest/smallest/most expensive to slowest/largest/cheapest: registers, L1/L2/L3 cache, RAM, SSD/disk
Each level caches data from the level below
Temporal locality: recently accessed data is likely to be accessed again soon (loop variables)
Spatial locality: data near recently accessed data is likely to be accessed soon (array traversal)
Caches load whole blocks (cache lines) to exploit spatial locality
High hit rates make the system almost as fast as the top level while being as large as the bottom
entries.referenceAnswer: Memory is organized as a hierarchy: registers, then CPU caches, then RAM, then SSD or disk. Each level down is larger and cheaper but slower. It works because programs have locality of reference. Temporal locality means something accessed recently will probably be accessed again soon, like a loop counter. Spatial locality means nearby data will probably be accessed soon, like the next element of an array. So caches keep recently used data and fetch whole cache lines at a time, and most accesses hit in the fast levels. The result feels almost as fast as the cache, with the capacity of RAM or disk. The same principle is why TLBs and page caching work.
commonMistakes: Mixing up temporal and spatial locality
Not explaining why caching gives a speed-up

questions: What is the difference between the long-term, short-term and medium-term schedulers?
What is the dispatcher, and what is dispatch latency?
keyPoints: Long-term (job) scheduler: decides which jobs are admitted into memory/the ready queue; controls the degree of multiprogramming; runs infrequently
The long-term scheduler should admit a good mix of I/O-bound and CPU-bound processes
Short-term (CPU) scheduler: picks which ready process runs next; runs very frequently, so it must be fast
Medium-term scheduler: swaps processes out of and back into memory (suspend/resume) to reduce load
Dispatcher: gives the CPU to the selected process: context switch, switch to user mode, jump to the right instruction
Dispatch latency: time taken by the dispatcher to stop one process and start another
entries.referenceAnswer: The long-term scheduler decides which jobs get admitted into memory at all, so it controls the degree of multiprogramming. It runs rarely and tries to admit a balanced mix of I/O-bound and CPU-bound work. The short-term scheduler, the CPU scheduler, picks which ready process runs next. It runs many times a second, so it has to be very fast. The medium-term scheduler temporarily swaps processes out of memory and later back in, to relieve memory pressure. Once the short-term scheduler has chosen, the dispatcher actually hands over the CPU: it performs the context switch, switches to user mode and jumps to where the process left off. The time that takes is the dispatch latency.
commonMistakes: Confusing the short-term scheduler with the dispatcher
Not knowing what the medium-term scheduler does

questions: What extra issues come up when scheduling on a multi-core system?
What is processor affinity, and why does it conflict with load balancing?
keyPoints: Symmetric multiprocessing (SMP): each core schedules itself, usually with per-core run queues
Processor affinity: keep a process on the same core to reuse its warm cache (soft affinity: preferred; hard affinity: pinned)
Load balancing: move work from busy cores to idle ones (push migration and pull migration)
Migration loses cache warmth, so affinity and load balancing pull in opposite directions
NUMA: memory access time depends on which CPU the memory is attached to, so the scheduler prefers running a process near its memory
entries.referenceAnswer: On multi-core systems the scheduler has to decide which process runs and also which core runs it. Most systems use symmetric multiprocessing with a run queue per core. Processor affinity means trying to keep a process on the same core, because that core's cache is already full of its data, and moving it means a burst of cache misses. But if one core is overloaded while another sits idle, you want load balancing, either pushing tasks away from busy cores or letting idle cores pull tasks. Those goals conflict: every migration improves balance but throws away cache warmth, so schedulers only migrate when the imbalance is significant. On NUMA machines it matters even more, since running far from your memory is slower.
commonMistakes: Thinking one global queue is always best
Not being able to explain why affinity helps performance

questions: What is the difference between hard and soft real-time systems?
Compare Rate Monotonic Scheduling and Earliest Deadline First.
keyPoints: Hard real-time: missing a deadline is a system failure (airbag controller, pacemaker)
Soft real-time: missing deadlines degrades quality but is tolerated (video streaming)
Rate Monotonic: static priorities; shorter period means higher priority; preemptive
RMS is guaranteed schedulable if CPU utilization is at most n(2^(1/n) - 1), which approaches about 69% for many tasks
EDF: dynamic priorities; the task with the nearest deadline runs first
EDF is optimal on a single processor: it can schedule any task set with total utilization up to 100%
entries.referenceAnswer: In a hard real-time system, missing a deadline counts as failure, like an airbag firing late. In a soft real-time system, occasional misses just reduce quality, like a dropped video frame. Rate Monotonic Scheduling assigns fixed priorities by period: the more frequently a task repeats, the higher its priority. It's simple and predictable, but it's only guaranteed to meet all deadlines if utilization stays under a bound that approaches about 69% as the number of tasks grows. Earliest Deadline First recalculates priorities dynamically and always runs whatever task's deadline is closest. On a single processor it's optimal and can use up to 100% of the CPU, at the cost of more runtime overhead and less predictable behaviour under overload.
