commonMistakes: Saying real-time means 'very fast'
Saying RMS priorities change at runtime

questions: What are signals in Unix/Linux?
What is the difference between SIGTERM and SIGKILL?
keyPoints: A signal is a software notification delivered asynchronously to a process
Examples: SIGINT (Ctrl+C), SIGTERM (polite termination request), SIGKILL (forced kill), SIGSEGV (invalid memory access), SIGCHLD (child changed state)
A process can handle a signal with a custom handler, ignore it, or take the default action
SIGKILL and SIGSTOP can't be caught, blocked or ignored
SIGTERM lets a program clean up (close files, flush data) before exiting; SIGKILL gives it no chance
Signal handlers must only call async-signal-safe functions
entries.referenceAnswer: Signals are the Unix way of asynchronously notifying a process that something happened, a bit like software interrupts. Pressing Ctrl+C sends SIGINT, an invalid memory access raises SIGSEGV, and a parent gets SIGCHLD when a child exits. For most signals a process can install a handler, ignore the signal, or accept the default action, which is often to terminate. SIGTERM is the polite request to stop: a well-behaved program catches it, saves its state, closes connections and exits cleanly, and that's what kill sends by default. SIGKILL can't be caught or ignored, so the kernel just ends the process immediately, with no cleanup. You use it only when SIGTERM doesn't work.
commonMistakes: Saying SIGKILL can be handled
Using kill -9 as the first choice

questions: What is a memory-mapped file?
Why can mmap be faster than read() and write() for file access?
keyPoints: mmap maps a file's contents into the process's virtual address space; the file is then accessed like memory
Pages are loaded lazily through page faults (demand paging)
Avoids an extra copy between a kernel buffer and a user buffer, and avoids a system call per access
Modified pages are marked dirty and written back to the file by the OS (or explicitly with msync)
Shared mappings let multiple processes share memory (a form of IPC)
The OS uses the same mechanism to load executables and shared libraries
entries.referenceAnswer: A memory-mapped file is a file mapped straight into a process's virtual address space, so reading and writing the file becomes ordinary memory access. mmap doesn't read the file up front. It just sets up page table entries, and the first touch of each page causes a page fault that loads it from disk. It can beat read() and write() because read copies data from the kernel's buffer into your buffer and costs a system call each time, while with mmap you work directly on the pages in the page cache. Modified pages get written back to the file by the OS. If two processes map the same file as shared, they see each other's changes, which is also a form of IPC. It's how the OS loads programs and shared libraries.
commonMistakes: Saying mmap reads the whole file into memory immediately
Not connecting mmap to page faults

questions: What is swapping, and how is it different from paging?
keyPoints: Swapping (classic): moving an entire process between main memory and a backing store (disk)
Done by the medium-term scheduler to free memory or reduce the degree of multiprogramming
Paging: moving individual fixed-size pages in and out as needed
Whole-process swapping is expensive because the transfer time is proportional to the process size
Modern systems mostly page; the disk area is still called swap space
entries.referenceAnswer: Swapping, in the classic sense, moves a whole process out of RAM to disk and later brings it back, which is what the medium-term scheduler does when memory is overcommitted. Paging works at a much finer grain: only the individual pages that are needed are loaded, and only individual pages get evicted. Moving entire processes is slow, since the transfer time grows with the process size, so modern systems page instead. The disk area they page to is still called swap space, which is why the terms get mixed up.
commonMistakes: Treating swapping and paging as exactly the same thing
Not knowing which scheduler performs swapping

questions: What are the trade-offs between small and large page sizes?
What are huge pages and when are they used?
keyPoints: Small pages: less internal fragmentation, finer-grained loading of only what's needed
Small pages: larger page tables and more TLB misses
Large pages: smaller page tables, greater TLB reach (fewer misses), efficient bulk disk I/O
Large pages: more internal fragmentation, and may load data that isn't needed
Typical page size is 4 KB; huge pages (e.g. 2 MB or 1 GB) are used by databases and VMs with large memory footprints to reduce TLB misses
entries.referenceAnswer: Page size is a trade-off. Small pages waste less memory to internal fragmentation, and let the OS load only the parts of a program actually used. But they mean more pages, so bigger page tables and more TLB misses, since each TLB entry covers less memory. Large pages flip that: smaller page tables and much better TLB coverage, but more wasted space in partially used pages and possibly loading data you don't need. Most systems use 4 KB pages by default, and offer huge pages of 2 MB or even 1 GB for workloads like databases and virtual machines, which touch huge amounts of memory and would otherwise suffer lots of TLB misses.
commonMistakes: Saying larger pages are always better
Not linking page size to TLB reach

questions: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?
Can you have concurrency on a single-core CPU?
keyPoints: Concurrency: multiple tasks make progress over overlapping time periods, possibly by interleaving
Parallelism: multiple tasks execute at literally the same instant on multiple cores/CPUs
Concurrency is possible on a single core through time slicing; parallelism needs multiple cores
Concurrency is about structuring a program as independent tasks; parallelism is about executing them simultaneously
Example: Node.js handles many requests concurrently on one thread using an event loop
entries.referenceAnswer: Concurrency means several tasks are in progress during the same period. They take turns, and their execution overlaps in time, but they don't necessarily run at the same instant. Parallelism means tasks really do run at the same moment, on different cores. So a single-core CPU can be concurrent, by switching between tasks quickly, but not parallel. Concurrency is about how you structure a program, as independent tasks. Parallelism is about how it's executed. Node.js is a good example: it handles thousands of requests concurrently on a single thread by switching between them whenever one waits for I/O, without any parallelism in the JavaScript itself.
commonMistakes: Using the two terms interchangeably
Saying concurrency requires multiple cores

questions: What is the difference between multiprogramming, multitasking and multiprocessing?
keyPoints: Multiprogramming: several programs kept in memory; when one waits for I/O, the CPU switches to another; goal: maximize CPU utilization
Multitasking (time-sharing): the CPU switches rapidly between tasks using time slices, so users get interactive response; goal: responsiveness
Multitasking is preemptive (a timer interrupt); classic multiprogramming switches only when a process blocks
Multiprocessing: a system with more than one CPU/core, so tasks can run in parallel
Multithreading: multiple threads within one process
entries.referenceAnswer: Multiprogramming keeps several programs in memory so the CPU is never idle: when the running program waits for I/O, the CPU switches to another one. Its goal is utilization. Multitasking, or time-sharing, extends that by also switching on a timer, giving each task a short time slice, so many interactive users or programs all feel responsive. Its goal is response time. Multiprocessing is about hardware: having two or more CPUs, so work can actually run in parallel. Multithreading is multiple threads of execution inside a single process.
commonMistakes: Treating multiprogramming and multiprocessing as the same
Saying multitasking requires multiple CPUs

questions: What are the different types of operating systems?
Where would you use a real-time operating system?
keyPoints: Batch OS: jobs grouped and run without user interaction (early mainframes)
Time-sharing/multitasking OS: many interactive users/tasks share the CPU (Linux, Windows)
Real-time OS (RTOS): guarantees responses within deadlines (medical devices, automotive, industrial control)
Distributed OS: manages a group of networked computers so they appear as one system
Network OS: provides file/printer sharing and user management across a network
Embedded and mobile OS: for resource-constrained devices (Android, iOS, firmware)
entries.referenceAnswer: Early batch systems ran queued jobs one after another with no user interaction. Time-sharing systems, like Linux and Windows today, rapidly switch the CPU among many tasks so interactive use feels smooth. Real-time operating systems guarantee that tasks respond within strict deadlines, which is why they're used in things like car braking systems, pacemakers and industrial robots, where being late is as bad as being wrong. Distributed operating systems make a cluster of machines look like a single system, network operating systems focus on sharing resources across a network, and embedded and mobile operating systems are tuned for limited hardware and battery life.
commonMistakes: Saying a real-time OS is simply a faster OS
Confusing distributed and network operating systems

questions: What is the difference between buffering, caching and spooling?
Why does printing use spooling?
keyPoints: Buffer: temporary storage for data being transferred, to cope with speed or transfer-size mismatches between devices
Double buffering lets one buffer be filled while the other is emptied
Cache: a fast copy of data whose original lives elsewhere, kept to speed up future access
A buffer may hold the only copy of the data; a cache always holds a copy
Spooling: a buffer (usually on disk) holding output for a device that can serve only one job at a time, e.g. a printer
Spooling lets many processes 'print' at once while the printer receives jobs one by one without interleaving
entries.referenceAnswer: A buffer is temporary memory used while moving data between two things that work at different speeds or in different chunk sizes, like a network card and an application. Double buffering fills one buffer while the other drains. A cache is different: it's a faster copy of data that also exists somewhere else, kept so repeated accesses are quick. A buffer may hold the only copy, a cache never does. Spooling is a special buffer, usually on disk, for devices that can only handle one job at a time. With printing, many programs can send documents at once. They're written to the spool as separate jobs, and the printer takes them one at a time, so pages from different documents never get mixed together.
commonMistakes: Using buffer and cache as synonyms
Not being able to explain why spooling is needed

questions: What is the difference between a virtual machine and a container like Docker?
What is a hypervisor? What is the difference between type 1 and type 2 hypervisors?
keyPoints: A VM virtualizes the hardware: each VM runs its own full guest OS kernel on top of a hypervisor
Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor runs directly on hardware (VMware ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM); Type 2 (hosted) runs on a host OS (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation)
A container virtualizes at the OS level: containers share the host's kernel and are isolated processes
Linux containers use namespaces (isolation of PIDs, network, file system) and cgroups (resource limits)
Containers are lightweight: they start in seconds or less, use less memory, and package an app with its dependencies
VMs give stronger isolation and can run a different OS kernel (e.g. Windows on Linux)
entries.referenceAnswer: A virtual machine emulates a whole computer. A hypervisor sits under it, and each VM boots its own complete guest operating system with its own kernel. A type 1 hypervisor like KVM or ESXi runs directly on the hardware, and a type 2 like VirtualBox runs as an application on a normal OS. A container is much lighter: it's really just a group of isolated processes that share the host's kernel. On Linux, namespaces give each container its own view of process IDs, network and files, and cgroups limit how much CPU and memory it can use. So containers start almost instantly, use far less memory, and package an app with its dependencies, which is why Docker is used for deployment. VMs give stronger isolation and let you run a completely different OS, since they don't share a kernel.
commonMistakes: Saying each container runs its own kernel
Saying containers are just lightweight VMs with no difference in isolation

questions: What is the difference between a reentrant function and a thread-safe function?
Can a function be thread-safe but not reentrant?
keyPoints: Thread-safe: works correctly when called from multiple threads at the same time (may achieve this using locks)
Reentrant: can be interrupted in the middle and safely called again (e.g. from a signal handler or recursion) before the first call finishes
Reentrant functions use no static or global mutable state and call only reentrant functions; they work only with their parameters and local variables
A function that uses a mutex is thread-safe but not reentrant: if it's interrupted while holding the lock and re-entered, it deadlocks
Example: strtok keeps static state (neither); strtok_r takes the state as a parameter (reentrant)
entries.referenceAnswer: A thread-safe function behaves correctly when several threads call it at the same time, and it can achieve that by using locks around shared state. A reentrant function is stricter: it can be interrupted partway through, for example by a signal handler, and called again before the first call finishes, and both calls still work. That basically requires it to use only its parameters and local variables, no static or global mutable state. So a function can be thread-safe but not reentrant. If it protects shared data with a mutex and a signal handler interrupts it while it holds the lock and calls it again, the second call waits forever for a lock that can never be released. strtok is the classic example: it keeps hidden static state, so it's neither, which is why strtok_r, which takes that state as a parameter, exists.
commonMistakes: Treating the two terms as identical
Saying adding a lock makes a function reentrant

questions: What is a journaling file system, and what problem does it solve?
What happens to the file system if power fails in the middle of a write?
keyPoints: A single file operation (e.g. creating a file) updates several on-disk structures: inode, bitmap, directory entry, data blocks
A crash in the middle can leave these inconsistent (e.g. an allocated block not owned by any file)
Without journaling, fsck must scan the entire disk after a crash, which is very slow on large disks
Journaling: first write the intended changes to a log (journal) and commit them, then apply them to their real locations
On recovery, replay committed journal transactions and discard incomplete ones, so recovery is fast
Modes: metadata-only (ordered, the ext4 default) vs full data journaling; copy-on-write file systems (ZFS, Btrfs) are an alternative
entries.referenceAnswer: Even a simple operation like creating a file touches several disk structures: the free-block bitmap, the inode, the directory entry and the data blocks. If power fails halfway through, they can disagree. For example, a block is marked used but no file points to it. Older systems ran fsck after a crash to scan and repair the whole disk, which can take a very long time on large disks. A journaling file system borrows the database idea of write-ahead logging: it first writes the set of changes it's about to make to a journal and marks it committed, and only then applies the changes to their real locations. After a crash, it replays any committed transactions from the journal and ignores incomplete ones, so recovery takes seconds. ext4 by default journals only metadata, while copy-on-write file systems like ZFS avoid the problem by never overwriting data in place.
commonMistakes: Saying journaling guarantees that no user data is ever lost
Not knowing why fsck is slow
